title: You Think Short-Term Memory Is One Box, Yet Eight Digits Proved It Has Four Rooms
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — Baddeley & Hitch (1974): Holding 8 Random Digits While Reasoning — Why Short-Term Memory Is a 4-Room Workshop, Not One Shelf, grounded in Alan D. Baddeley, Graham Hitch (1974) (Psychology of Learning and Motivation). Empirical findings show that by 1970, Atkinson & Shiffrin's textbook model taught that human Short-Term Memory (STM) was ONE single 7-slot shelf: if a neurological patient (like Patient K.F., who could barely repeat 2 digits after a left parietal lesion!) lost that shelf, their thinking and long-term learning should have collapsed — yet K.F. reasoned, learned, and lived normally.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how Broca's area, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, parietal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that in 1974 (Psychology of Learning and Motivation), Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch simulated being 'Patient K.F.' in healthy volunteers: fill their '7-slot shelf' completely to the brim by making them recite 6 to 8 random digits aloud non-stop, and AT THE SAME TIME test complex grammatical reasoning ('A is NOT preceded by B — BA: True or False?'), prose comprehension, and word recall.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Alan D. Baddeley, Graham Hitch (1974). Working Memory. Psychology of Learning and Motivation. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0079-7421(08)60452-1
- Alan D. Baddeley, Graham J. Hitch (2000). Development of Working Memory: Should the Pascual-Leone and the Baddeley and Hitch Models Be Merged? Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1006/jecp.2000.2592
- Cynthia He (2021). The challenge of ‘holding space’ while holding the pager. Current Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.12788/cp.0150
